> [!TLDR]
> Ingoing and outgoing Eddington–Finkelstein coordinates remove the horizon coordinate singularity while covering different pairs of Kruskal regions.

<!-- Source: PDF page 183, printed page 167. -->

Because of the implicit nature of the relation between $\mechanical{r}$ and $\mechanical{U}\mechanical{V}$, the Kruskal coordinates can be awkward to use in some computations. In fact, it is rarely necessary to employ coordinates that cover all four regions of the Kruskal diagram, although it is often desirable to have coordinates that are well behaved at $\mechanical{r}=2\mechanical{M}$. In such situations, choosing $\mechanical{v}$ and $\mechanical{r}$ as coordinates, or $\mechanical{u}$ and $\mechanical{r}$, does the trick. These coordinate systems are called *ingoing* and *outgoing Eddington–Finkelstein* coordinates, respectively.

It is easy to check that in the ingoing coordinates, the Schwarzschild metric takes the form

$$
\mathrm d\mechanical{s}^2=-(1-2\mechanical{M}/\mechanical{r})\mathrm d\mechanical{v}^2
+2\,\mathrm d\mechanical{v}\,\mathrm d\mechanical{r}+\mechanical{r}^2\mathrm d\Omega^2, \tag{5.10}
$$

while in the outgoing coordinates,

$$
\mathrm d\mechanical{s}^2=-(1-2\mechanical{M}/\mechanical{r})\mathrm d\mechanical{u}^2
-2\,\mathrm d\mechanical{u}\,\mathrm d\mechanical{r}+\mechanical{r}^2\mathrm d\Omega^2. \tag{5.11}
$$

It may also be verified that the $(\mechanical{v},\mechanical{r})$ coordinates cover regions **I** and **II** of the Kruskal diagram, while $\mechanical{u}$ and $\mechanical{r}$ cover regions **IV** and **I**.

The Eddington–Finkelstein coordinates can also be used to construct spacetime diagrams (Fig. 5.3), but these do not have the property that both ingoing and outgoing null geodesics propagate at 45 degrees. For example, it follows from Eq. (5.10) that ingoing light rays move with $\mathrm d\mechanical{v}=0$, that is, along coordinate lines that can be oriented at 45 degrees, but the outgoing rays move with $\mathrm d\mechanical{v}/\mathrm d\mechanical{r}=2/(1-2\mechanical{M}/\mechanical{r})$, that is, with a varying slope.

## Physical quantities

| Symbol | Unit | Quantity | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\mechanical{M}$ | $\unit{\mathrm{m}}$ | Mass | The Schwarzschild black-hole mass. |
| $\mechanical{r}$ | $\unit{\mathrm{m}}$ | Radius | The spherical areal radius. |
| $\mechanical{u},\mechanical{v}$ | $\unit{\mathrm{m}}$ | Null times | The retarded and advanced time coordinates. |
| $\mechanical{U},\mechanical{V}$ | $1$ | Kruskal coordinates | The dimensionless null coordinates of the extended spacetime. |
| $\mechanical{s}$ | $\unit{\mathrm{m}}$ | Interval | The Schwarzschild line element in the null-time coordinates. |
